children.name: Setophaga
children.description: The typical wood-warblers — a large and diverse genus of small, insectivorous passerines that forms the core of the Parulidae. Males in breeding plumage display bold patterns of yellow, black, white, blue, and chestnut; females and non-breeding birds are more subdued. They are among the most sought-after birds by North American birders during spring migration, when males sing from treetops in brilliant breeding colours.

children.name: Setophaga ruticilla
children.description: The American redstart (Setophaga ruticilla) is a New World warbler.

children.name: Setophaga petechia
children.description: The yellow warbler (Setophaga petechia) is a New World warbler species.

children.name: Setophaga coronata
children.description:
The yellow-rumped warbler (Setophaga coronata) is a regular North American bird species that can be commonly observed all across the continent. Its extensive range connects both the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of the U.S. As well as Canada and Central America, with the population concentrated in the continent's northern reaches during the breeding season and migrating southwards to southern North and Central America in the winter. It generally prefers coniferous forests or mixed coniferous-deciduous forests as its breeding habitat, while during the winter it can be found inhabiting more open areas such as shrublands that offer food resources. The yellow-rumped warbler is primarily insectivorous, though the species does eat fruits such as juniper berries as well, especially in winter.
The species combines four closely related forms: the eastern myrtle warbler (spp. Coronata); its western counterpart, Audubon's warbler (spp. Group auduboni); the northwest Mexican black-fronted warbler (spp. Nigrifrons); and the Guatemalan Goldman's warbler (spp. Goldmani). All subspecies of the yellow-rumped warbler are characterized by the yellow rump as its name implies, while intra-group and inter-group variations in appearance exist in spite of many similarities. The myrtle and Audubon's groups, as two major subspecies, are distinguished by noticeable features such as differing throat colorations.

children.name: Setophaga caerulescens
children.description:
The black-throated blue warbler (Setophaga caerulescens) is a small passerine bird of the New World warbler family. Its breeding ranges are located in the interior of deciduous and mixed coniferous forests in eastern North America. Over the cooler months, it migrates to islands in the Caribbean and Central America. It is very rarely found in western Europe, where it is considered to be a non-indigenous species. The black-throated blue warbler is sexually dimorphic; the adult male has a black face and cheeks, deep blue upperparts and white underparts, while the adult female is olive-brown above and light yellow below.
Predominantly insectivorous, the black-throated blue warbler supplements its diet with berries and seeds in winter. It builds its nests in thick shrubs and the closeness of its nesting sites to the ground make it a favored species for the study of warbler behavior in the wild. The black-throated blue warbler defends its territory against other birds of the same species for both nesting and winter habitats. As the black-throated blue warbler requires large, unbroken forest areas for nesting, its numbers are declining.

children.name: Setophaga fusca
children.description: The Blackburnian warbler (Setophaga fusca) is a small New World warbler.

children.name: Setophaga americana
children.description: The northern parula (Setophaga americana) is a small New World warbler.

children.name: Setophaga magnolia
children.description: The magnolia warbler (Setophaga magnolia) is a member of the wood warbler family Parulidae.

children.name: Setophaga striata
children.description: The blackpoll warbler (Setophaga striata) is a New World warbler.

children.name: Setophaga virens
children.description: The black-throated green warbler (Setophaga virens) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family.

children.name: Setophaga townsendi
children.description: Townsend's warbler (Setophaga townsendi) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family.

children.name: Setophaga occidentalis
children.description: The hermit warbler (Setophaga occidentalis) is a small perching bird.

children.name: Setophaga graciae
children.description: Grace's warbler (Setophaga graciae) is a small New World warbler that specializes in pine woods.

children.name: Setophaga dominica
children.description: The yellow-throated warbler (Setophaga dominica) is a small migratory songbird species in the New World warbler family (Parulidae) found in temperate North America.

children.name: Setophaga palmarum
children.description: The palm warbler (Setophaga palmarum) is a small songbird in the New World warbler family.

children.name: Setophaga discolor
children.description: The prairie warbler (Setophaga discolor) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family.

children.name: Setophaga castanea
children.description: The bay-breasted warbler (Setophaga castanea) is a small species of songbird in the New World warbler family, Parulidae. It is one of 35 species in the diverse genus Setophaga. Like all songbirds, or passerines, the species is classified in the order Passeriformes.

children.name: Setophaga cerulea
children.description: The cerulean warbler (Setophaga cerulea) is a small songbird in the family Parulidae.

children.name: Setophaga pensylvanica
children.description: The chestnut-sided warbler (Setophaga pensylvanica) is a New World warbler. They breed in eastern North America and in southern Canada westwards to the Canadian Prairies. They also breed in the Great Lakes region and in the eastern United States.

children.name: Setophaga tigrina
children.description: The Cape May warbler (Setophaga tigrina) is a species of New World warbler. It breeds in northern North America. Its breeding range spans all but the westernmost parts of southern Canada, the Great Lakes region, and New England. It is migratory, wintering in the West Indies. This species is a very rare vagrant to western Europe, with two records in Britain as of October 2013. The English name refers to Cape May, New Jersey, where George Ord collected the specimen that was later described by Alexander Wilson.

children.name: Setophaga pinus
children.description: The pine warbler (Setophaga pinus) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family Parulidae.

children.name: Setophaga kirtlandii
children.description:
Kirtland's warbler (Setophaga kirtlandii), also known in Michigan by the common name jack pine bird, or the jack pine warbler, is a small songbird of the New World warbler family (Parulidae). Nearly extinct just years ago, populations have recovered due to the conservation efforts of the Kirtland's Warbler Conservation Team and its members. The birds require large areas, greater than 160 acres (65 hectares), of dense young jack pine for breeding habitat. This habitat was historically created by wildfire, but today is created through the harvest of mature jack pine (Pinus banksiana), and planting of jack pine seedlings.
The population of the species spends the spring and summer in its breeding range in the Great Lakes region of Canada (Ontario) and the United States (Wisconsin and Michigan, especially in the northeastern Lower Peninsula), and winters in the West Indies.

children.name: Setophaga adelaidae
children.description: Adelaide's warbler (Setophaga adelaidae), or reinita mariposera (in Puerto Rican Spanish) is a bird endemic to the archipelago of Puerto Rico belonging to the genus Setophaga of the family Parulidae (New World warblers).

children.name: Setophaga subita
children.description: The Barbuda warbler (Setophaga subita) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae.

children.name: Setophaga delicata
children.description: The Saint Lucia warbler (Setophaga delicata) is a species of passerine bird belonging to the family Parulidae, the New World warblers. This species is endemic to Saint Lucia. It was formerly considered a subspecies of the Adelaide's warbler.

children.name: Setophaga pharetra
children.description: }} The arrowhead warbler (Setophaga pharetra) is a species of passerine in the family Parulidae, endemic to Jamaica.

children.name: Setophaga plumbea
children.description: | range_map = Dendroica plumbea map.svg }}.

children.name: Setophaga angelae
children.description:
The elfin woods warbler (Setophaga angelae) is a species of bird endemic to Puerto Rico, where it is local and uncommon. Discovered in 1968 and described in 1972, it is the most recently described New World warbler (family Parulidae).
The species name, angelae, is a tribute to Angela Kepler, one of its discoverers. These birds are insectivores, as they feed by gleaning small insects off the habitat leaves.

children.name: Setophaga chrysoparia
children.description: The golden-cheeked warbler (Setophaga chrysoparia) is an endangered species of bird that breeds in Central Texas, from Palo Pinto County southwestward along the eastern and southern edge of the Edwards Plateau to Kinney County. The golden-cheeked warbler is the only bird species with a breeding range endemic to Texas.

children.name: Setophaga pityophila
children.description: The olive-capped warbler (Setophaga pityophila) is a species of New World warbler that is native to the western and eastern ends of Cuba as well as Grand Bahama and the Abaco Islands in the Bahamas. Its natural habitat is pine forests and occasionally adjacent mixed forests.

children.name: Setophaga flavescens
children.description: The Bahama warbler (Setophaga flavescens) is an endangered species of bird in the family Parulidae that is endemic to The Bahamas.

children.name: Setophaga vitellina
children.description: The vitelline warbler (Setophaga vitellina) is a songbird species in the New World warbler family (Parulidae).

children.name: Setophaga nigrescens
children.description: The black-throated gray warbler or black-throated grey warbler (Setophaga nigrescens) is a passerine bird of the New World warbler family Parulidae. It is long and has gray and white plumage with black markings. The male has the bold black throat of its name, and black stripes on its head, as well as black streaks on its flanks; the female is a paler version of the male, with a white throat and less distinct black markings on the flanks and wings. It breeds in western North America from British Columbia to New Mexico, and winters in Mexico and the southwestern United States. The habitats it prefers are coniferous and mixed forests and scrubland, especially those with pinyon pines, junipers, sagebrush, and oaks. Its nest is an open cup of plant fibers lined with feathers, built a few metres from the ground in the branches of a tree or shrub. Three to five eggs are laid, and young are fed by both parents. Common in its breeding range, it does not seem to be seriously threatened by human activities, unlike many migratory warblers.

children.name: Setophaga pitiayumi
children.description: The tropical parula (Setophaga pitiayumi) is a small New World warbler.

children.name: Setophaga batesii
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with distinctive white eye ring and a short tail. Known for its melodious song, this species can be found in dense evergreen forests along the Pacific Northwest coast.

children.name: Geothlypis flavida
children.description: A small, greenish warbler with a bright yellow throat and breast. Known for its loud, high-pitched calls during the breeding season, this species is found in deciduous forests and woodlands.

children.name: Protonotaria grisea
children.description: A small, olive-brown warbler with a strikingly white throat and underparts. Known for its distinctive hooting song, this species is found in wooded swamps and wetlands of the southeastern United States.

children.name: Seiurus ohiensis
children.description: A small, brown warbler with a distinctive white band across the breast and yellow flanks. Known for its steady hopping on the ground in search of insect prey, this species is found along streams and rivers in eastern North America.

children.name: Mniotilta vellei
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a bright white throat and breast. Known for its loud, raspy calls during the breeding season, this species is found in forests along the Atlantic coast.

children.name: Parkesia albifrons
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a yellow breast and belly. Known for its distinctive call that sounds like the bark of an old oak tree, this species is found in deciduous forests.

children.name: Cardellina leucophrys
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a bright white throat and breast. Known for its loud, buzzy song during the breeding season, this species is found in coastal wetlands.

children.name: Leiothlypis brevicauda
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a white eyebrow and breast. Known for its high-pitched trills during the breeding season, this species is found in open woodlands.

children.name: Oporornis dominica
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a white throat and breast. Known for its loud, whistling song during the breeding season, this species is found in coastal forests.

children.name: Vermivora cinerea
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a black throat and breast. Known for its distinctive call that sounds like “cheer cheer,” this species is found in deciduous forests.

children.name: Myioborus lucernarius
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a white throat and breast. Known for its melodious song during the breeding season, this species is found in coastal forests of South America.

children.name: Basileuterus rufogularis
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a rufous throat and breast. Known for its distinctive call that sounds like “chip chip,” this species is found in tropical forests.

children.name: Myiothlypis fulvogularis
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a yellow throat and breast. Known for its melodious song during the breeding season, this species is found in coastal forests of South America.

children.name: Oreothlypis nigriceps
children.description: A small, olive-green warbler with a black throat and breast. Known for its loud, raspy calls during the breeding season, this species is found in coastal forests.

children.name: Geothlypis
children.description: The yellowthroats — a genus of stocky, skulking warblers of dense, wet vegetation. Males are distinguished by a bold black mask across the face, bordered above by a white or grey band. They are more often heard than seen, delivering a loud, repetitive 'wichity-wichity-wichity' song from the depths of cattail marshes and brushy swamps.

children.name: Geothlypis trichas
children.description: The common yellowthroat (Geothlypis trichas) is a New World warbler.

children.name: Geothlypis formosa
children.description: The Kentucky warbler (Geothlypis formosa) is a small species of New World warbler.

children.name: Geothlypis philadelphia
children.description: The mourning warbler (Geothlypis philadelphia) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family.

children.name: Geothlypis tolmiei
children.description:
MacGillivray's warbler (Geothlypis tolmiei) is a species of New World warbler. These birds are sluggish and heavy warblers, preferring to spend most of their time on, or near the ground, except when singing.
MacGillivray's warbler was named by John James Audubon in honor of Scottish ornithologist William MacGillivray, although the proper credit to its discovery goes to John Kirk Townsend. The specific name was given in honor of William Fraser Tolmie.

children.name: Geothlypis beldingi
children.description:
Belding's yellowthroat (Geothlypis beldingi) is a New World warbler. It is a resident breeder endemic to the southern Baja California Peninsula (Mexico).
It is closely related to common yellowthroat, Altamira yellowthroat and Bahama yellowthroat, with which it forms a superspecies, and was formerly considered conspecific.

children.name: Geothlypis flavovelata
children.description: The Altamira yellowthroat (Geothlypis flavovelata) is a New World warbler.

children.name: Geothlypis rostrata
children.description: The Bahama yellowthroat (Geothlypis rostrata) is a New World warbler.

children.name: Geothlypis speciosa
children.description: The black-polled yellowthroat (Geothlypis speciosa) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae.

children.name: Geothlypis aequinoctialis
children.description: The masked yellowthroat (Geothlypis aequinoctialis) is a New World warbler.

children.name: Geothlypis poliocephala
children.description: The grey-crowned yellowthroat (Geothlypis poliocephala) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It is found in Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, and the United States. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist shrubland and heavily degraded former forest.

children.name: Geothlypis semiflava
children.description: The olive-crowned yellowthroat (Geothlypis semiflava) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It is found in Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua, and Panama. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist shrubland and heavily degraded former forest.

children.name: Protonotaria
children.description: The prothonotary warbler — a monotypic genus of cavity-nesting warbler named for the golden-yellow robes of papal notaries. It is one of only two Parulidae species that nest in tree cavities, and the only eastern North American warbler to do so. Its brilliant colouration and gentle song make it one of the most prized species among birders.

children.name: Protonotaria citrea
children.description: The prothonotary warbler (Protonotaria citrea) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family.

children.name: Seiurus
children.description: The ovenbird — a monotypic genus of large, terrestrial warbler named for its distinctive domed nest, which resembles a dutch oven. It is one of the few warblers that forages entirely on the forest floor, walking deliberately in search of invertebrates. Its loud, ringing 'teacher-TEACHER-TEACHER' song is one of the most powerful and distinctive sounds of eastern North American forests.

children.name: Seiurus aurocapilla
children.description: The ovenbird (Seiurus aurocapilla) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family Parulidae. It is the only species placed in the genus Seiurus. This migratory bird breeds in eastern North America and winters in Central America, many Caribbean islands, Florida and northern Venezuela.

children.name: Mniotilta
children.description: The black-and-white warbler — a distinctive monotypic genus with a unique foraging behaviour that sets it apart from all other Parulidae. It creeps along tree trunks and branches like a nuthatch, probing bark crevices for hidden insects. Its black-and-white streaked plumage resembles that of a tiny woodpecker, and its squeaky, wheel-like song is a familiar sound of North American woodlands.

children.name: Mniotilta varia
children.description: The black-and-white warbler (Mniotilta varia) is a species of New World warbler, and the only member of its genus, Mniotilta. It breeds in northern and eastern North America and winters in Florida, Central America, and the West Indies down to Peru. It has been recorded as a vagrant in Northern Europe, especially Britain and Ireland. Relative to other New World warblers, it is not well studied.

children.name: Parkesia
children.description: The waterthrushes — a small genus of large, terrestrial warblers restricted to wet habitats. They resemble thrushes in build and behaviour, with heavily streaked underparts and a habit of bobbing their rear body. They walk on the ground along streams and in swamps, flipping dead leaves in search of insects, and are among the most secretive of North American warblers despite their size.

children.name: Parkesia noveboracensis
children.description: The northern waterthrush (Parkesia noveboracensis) It is a rare vagrant to other South American countries and to western Europe.

children.name: Cardellina
children.description: A small genus of colourful warblers with predominantly red or yellow plumage, including the redstarts and the Canada Warbler. They are active, acrobatic foragers of montane and boreal forests across the Americas.

children.name: Cardellina canadensis
children.description: The Canada warbler (Cardellina canadensis) is a small boreal songbird of the New World warbler family (Parulidae).

children.name: Cardellina pusilla
children.description: Wilson's warbler (Cardellina pusilla) is a small New World warbler. It is greenish above and yellow below, with rounded wings and a long, slim tail. The male has a black crown patch; depending on the subspecies, that mark is reduced or absent in the female. It breeds across Canada and south through the western United States, and winters from Mexico south through much of Central America. It is a very rare vagrant to western Europe.

children.name: Cardellina rubrifrons
children.description:
The red-faced warbler (Cardellina rubrifrons) is a species of New World warbler.
Mature red-faced warblers are small birds, long. They are light gray on top with a white rump and a white underside. The face, neck, and upper breast are all bright red, while the crown and sides of the head are black. The spot on the back of the head where the black crown and gray back meet is sometimes speckled gray, or sometimes plain white. They have a quirky habit of flicking their tail sideways while feeding.

children.name: Leiothlypis
children.description: A genus of small, plain-faced warblers with thin pointed bills and predominantly olive or grey upperparts. They forage deliberately in trees and shrubs, and are among the most common Neotropical migrants in North America.

children.name: Leiothlypis peregrina
children.description: The Tennessee warbler (Leiothlypis peregrina) is a New World warbler that breeds in eastern North America and winters in southern Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America.

children.name: Leiothlypis celata
children.description: The orange-crowned warbler (Leiothlypis celata) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family.

children.name: Leiothlypis ruficapilla
children.description: The Nashville warbler (Leiothlypis ruficapilla) is a small songbird in the New World warbler family, found in North and Central America.

children.name: Leiothlypis virginiae
children.description:
Virginia's warbler (Leiothlypis virginiae) is a species of New World warbler.
Despite what its name may suggest, Virginia's warbler is not actually named after the American State of Virginia, which makes sense as the birds' typical range only reaches as far east as the state of Texas. The bird's common eastern range is central and southern mountains of Colorado, central Wyoming, and central and western New Mexico. The bird was named for Virginia Anderson, the wife of an army surgeon who discovered the bird at Fort Burgwin, New Mexico, in 1858. When Spencer Fullerton Baird of the Smithsonian Institution fully described the bird for science in 1860 he honored the wishes of the warbler's discoverer and designated Virginia to be both the bird's common and scientific name.

children.name: Leiothlypis crissalis
children.description: The Colima warbler (Leiothlypis crissalis) is a New World warbler.

children.name: Leiothlypis luciae
children.description: Lucy's warbler (Leiothlypis luciae) is a small New World warbler found in North America. This species ranges includes southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico. It is one of only two warblers to nest in cavities.

children.name: Oporornis
children.description: A monotypic genus of secretive, skulking warbler with a preference for wet boreal forests and bogs. It is more often heard than seen, delivering its distinctive song from deep within dense spruce and tamarack stands.

children.name: Oporornis agilis
children.description: The Connecticut warbler (Oporornis agilis) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family.

children.name: Vermivora
children.description: A small genus of brightly coloured warblers with bold wing patterns and relatively large bills. They are among the most sought-after warblers by birders due to their striking beauty and the conservation concern surrounding some species.

children.name: Vermivora cyanoptera
children.description: The blue-winged warbler (Vermivora cyanoptera) is a fairly common migratory New World warbler, long and. It breeds in eastern North America in southern Ontario and the eastern United States and winters in southern Central America. Its breeding range is extending northwards, where it is replacing the very closely related golden-winged warbler (Vermivora chrysoptera).

children.name: Vermivora chrysoptera
children.description: The golden-winged warbler (Vermivora chrysoptera) is a small migratory insectivorous bird in the New World warbler family Parulidae. It breeds in southeastern and south-central Canada and in the Appalachian Mountains in the northeastern to north-central United States. The majority (~70%) of the global population breeds in Wisconsin, Minnesota, and Manitoba. Golden-winged warbler populations are slowly expanding northwards but are generally declining across its range. This is most likely as a result of habitat loss and competition/interbreeding with the very closely related blue-winged warbler, Vermivora cyanoptera, albeit the latter point has been debated. Populations are now restricted to two regions: the Great Lakes and the Appalachian Mountains.

children.name: Myioborus
children.description: The whitestarts or redstarts — a genus of brightly coloured warblers with vivid red, yellow, and black plumage and distinctive white outer tail feathers that are constantly fanned. They are active, acrobatic foragers of montane forests from the southwestern United States through the Andes.

children.name: Myioborus pictus
children.description: The painted redstart or painted whitestart (Myioborus pictus) is a species of New World warbler found in mountainous areas across inland Central America.

children.name: Myioborus miniatus
children.description: The slate-throated whitestart (Myioborus miniatus), also known as the slate-throated redstart, is a small insectivorous bird in the New World warbler family Parulidae that is native to Central and South America.

children.name: Myioborus ornatus
children.description: The golden-fronted whitestart (Myioborus ornatus) or the golden-fronted redstart, is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It is found in forest, woodland and scrub in the Andes of Colombia and far western Venezuela.

children.name: Myioborus albifrons
children.description: The white-fronted whitestart or white-fronted redstart (Myioborus albifrons) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It is endemic to forest and woodland in the Andes in western Venezuela. It is threatened by habitat loss.

children.name: Myioborus torquatus
children.description: The collared whitestart (Myioborus torquatus), also known as the collared redstart, is a tropical New World warbler endemic to the mountains of Costa Rica and western-central Panama.

children.name: Myioborus flavivertex
children.description: The yellow-crowned whitestart (Myioborus flavivertex), Santa Marta whitestart or yellow-crowned redstart, is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It is endemic to the highland forest and woodland in the Santa Marta Mountains in Colombia.

children.name: Myioborus albifacies
children.description: The white-faced whitestart or white-faced redstart (Myioborus albifacies) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It is endemic to humid highland forests in the tepuis of south-western Venezuela. Due to its isolated range, it is very poorly known.

children.name: Myioborus cardonai
children.description: The Guaiquinima whitestart (Myioborus cardonai), also known as the Guaiquinima redstart, saffron-breasted whitestart or saffron-breasted redstart, is a species of bird in the family Parulidae.

children.name: Myioborus brunniceps
children.description: The brown-capped whitestart or brown-capped redstart (Myioborus brunniceps) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It is found in humid Andean forests and woodlands in Bolivia and north-western Argentina. It sometimes includes the tepui whitestart as a subspecies.

children.name: Myioborus castaneocapillus
children.description: The tepui whitestart or tepui redstart (Myioborus castaneocapilla) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae.

children.name: Myioborus melanocephalus
children.description: The spectacled whitestart or spectacled redstart (Myioborus melanocephalus) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae.

children.name: Myioborus pariae
children.description: The Paria whitestart (Myioborus pariae), also known as the Paria redstart, yellow-faced whitestart or yellow-faced redstart, is a passerine bird of the New World warbler family, Parulidae.

children.name: Basileuterus
children.description: A genus of small, active warblers with bold head patterns, predominantly found in Central and South America. They are known for their bright colouration, including yellow, olive, and chestnut, often with striking crown stripes and supercilia.

children.name: Basileuterus culicivorus
children.description: The golden-crowned warbler (Basileuterus culicivorus) is a small insectivorous bird in the New World warbler family Parulidae. It has a large geographic range that extends from northeastern Mexico south to northern Argentina. The white-bellied warbler was formerly treated as a separate species but is now considered to be conspecific with the golden-crowned warbler.

children.name: Basileuterus trifasciatus
children.description: The three-banded warbler (Basileuterus trifasciatus) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It is found in Ecuador and Peru. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist montane forests and heavily degraded former forest.

children.name: Basileuterus tristriatus
children.description: The three-striped warbler (Basileuterus tristriatus) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It was previously considered conspecific with the Tacarcuna warbler and the black-eared warbler. It inhabits the northern Andes, from Venezuela to Peru. The Yungas warbler (Basileuterus punctipectus) was previously considered a subspecies.

children.name: Basileuterus melanotis
children.description: The black-eared warbler or Costa Rican warbler (Basileuterus melanotis) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It was previously considered conspecific with the three-striped warbler and the Tacarcuna warbler.

children.name: Basileuterus tacarcunae
children.description: The Tacarcuna warbler (Basileuterus tacarcunae) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae.

children.name: Basileuterus rufifrons
children.description:
The rufous-capped warbler (Basileuterus rufifrons) is a New World warbler native from Mexico south to Guatemala, rarely occurring as far north as southeastern Arizona and south Texas. Birds in the southern part of the range are now split out as a separate species, as the chestnut-capped warbler (Basileuterus delattrii).
Rufous-capped warblers generally reach a length of about. They are plain-olive to olive-gray, with white underbellies, bright yellow chests and throats, and a distinctive facial pattern consisting of a rufous cap, a white eyebrow-line (or superciliary), a dark eye-line fading into a rufous cheek, and a white malar marking. The bill is rather stout for a warbler, the wings are round and stubby, and the tail is long, often raised at a high angle and flicked.

children.name: Basileuterus melanogenys
children.description:
The black-cheeked warbler (Basileuterus melanogenys) is a New World warbler, resident breeding bird endemic to the Talamancan montane forests of Costa Rica and western Panama.
It is normally found in oak forests with a dense bamboo understory from 2500 m altitude to the timberline, but occasionally occurs as low as 1600 m. The breeding pair builds a bulky domed nest with a side entrance on a sloping bank or in a gully, and the female lays two white eggs.

children.name: Basileuterus ignotus
children.description: The Pirre warbler (Basileuterus ignotus) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae.

children.name: Basileuterus cabanisi
children.description: Cabanis's Warbler has a grey head, white supercilium, olive upperparts, and yellow underparts, found in the Andes from Peru to Bolivia. It inhabits the understorey of montane forests, often joining mixed-species flocks.

children.name: Myiothlypis
children.description: A genus of small warblers formerly included in Basileuterus, distinguished by their ground-foraging habits and often duller plumage. They are widespread in Central and South America, inhabiting forest understorey and edges.

children.name: Myiothlypis fulvicauda
children.description:
The buff-rumped warbler (Myiothlypis fulvicauda) is a New World warbler that is resident from Honduras south to northwestern Peru and disjunctly in the western Amazon. It is found in forests at up to 1500 m altitude, always near water.
The pair builds a bulky domed nest with a side entrance on a sloping bank next to a stream or path, and the female lays two white eggs which are incubated for 16–17 days with another 13–14 days to fledging.

children.name: Myiothlypis leucoblephara
children.description: The white-rimmed warbler or white-browed warbler (Myiothlypis leucoblephara) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It is found in Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist lowland forests, subtropical or tropical moist montane forests, subtropical or tropical moist shrubland, and heavily degraded former forest.

children.name: Myiothlypis rivularis
children.description: }} The riverbank warbler (Myiothlypis rivularis), sometimes known as the Neotropical river warbler or just "river warbler" (leading to confusion with Locustella fluviatilis), is a species of bird in the family Parulidae.

children.name: Myiothlypis bivittata
children.description: The two-banded warbler (Myiothlypis bivittata) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It is found in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Guyana, Peru, and Venezuela. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist montane forests and heavily degraded former forest.

children.name: Myiothlypis signata
children.description: The pale-legged warbler (Myiothlypis signata) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It is native to Argentina, Bolivia, Colombia and Peru. Its habitats include subtropical or tropical moist montane, as well as subtropical or tropical heavily degraded former forest.

children.name: Myiothlypis nigrocristata
children.description: The black-crested warbler (Myiothlypis nigrocristata) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It is found in Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist montane forests and heavily degraded former forest.

children.name: Myiothlypis luteoviridis
children.description: | range_map = Basileuterus luteoviridis map.svg.

children.name: Myiothlypis coronata
children.description: The russet-crowned warbler (Myiothlypis coronata) is a species of bird in the family Parulidae. It is found in Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist montane forests and heavily degraded former forest.

children.name: Myiothlypis flaveola
children.description: | range_map = Basileuterus flaveolus map.svg.

children.name: Myiothlypis blanchardes
children.description: Blanchard's Warbler has a grey head, white supercilium, olive upperparts, and pale underparts, found in the Paria Peninsula of Venezuela. It inhabits montane cloud forests and is classified as Near Threatened.

children.name: Myiothlypis mesoleuca
children.description: The White-bellied Warbler has olive-brown upperparts, a white belly, and a prominent white supercilium, found in the lowland forests of the Guiana Shield region.

children.name: Myiothlypis albifacies
children.description: The White-faced Warbler has a white face with a black crown, olive upperparts, and yellow underparts, found in the Andes of Peru and Bolivia.

children.name: Oreothlypis
children.description: A small genus of brightly coloured warblers with short tails and relatively large bills, found in highland forests from Mexico to Panama. They are active foragers that often join mixed-species flocks.

children.name: Oreothlypis superciliosa
children.description: The crescent-chested warbler (Oreothlypis superciliosa) is a small, New World warbler that is found throughout North and Central America from Texas to Nicaragua. This bird is similar to other warblers, however, certain features set them apart. This warbler is noticeable different than most warblers due to its brightly colored plumage and distinct features such as a white supercilium and orange crescent on its breast. Crescent-chested warblers create their nests near the ground and eggs are incubated by the female. Furthermore, there are differences in the plumage of these warblers depending on their age and sex such as down in young birds and more present crescents on male birds. These birds are foragers and eat insects. They are also migratory birds and normally survive in flocks. Lastly, the crescent-chested warbler has a number of predators including rodents and other avian predators.

children.name: Oreothlypis gutturalis
children.description: The flame-throated warbler (Oreothlypis gutturalis) is a small New World warbler. It is sometimes placed in the genera Vermivora and Parula.

children.name: Helmitheros
children.description: The worm-eating warbler — a monotypic genus of relatively large, terrestrial warbler named for its habit of eating caterpillars and other larvae. It has a distinctive striped head pattern and forages on the ground among dead leaves.

children.name: Helmitheros vermivorum
children.description: The worm-eating warbler (Helmitheros vermivorum) is a small New World warbler that breeds in the Eastern United States and migrates to southern Mexico, the Caribbean, and Central America for the winter. It is the only species in the genus Helmitheros.

children.name: Limnothlypis
children.description: A monotypic genus of large, secretive warbler named for its swamp habitat. It has a long bill and a distinctive habit of foraging among dead leaves and debris on the forest floor.

children.name: Limnothlypis swainsonii
children.description: Swainson's warbler (Limnothlypis swainsonii) is a small species of New World warbler. It is monotypic, the only member of the genus Limnothlypis. Swainson's warbler was named after William Swainson, an English ornithologist.

children.name: Euthlypis
children.description: The fan-tailed warbler — a monotypic genus of striking warbler with a long, constantly fanned tail. It is a skulking bird of forest understorey in Central America and Mexico.
